title: Gateway vs Mesh: Making the Call
summary: The decision framework interviewers actually probe — when you need a gateway, a mesh, or both.

slides.markdown:
Gateway and mesh aren't competitors — they solve traffic in **opposite directions**.

- **Gateway** = north-south, the system's edge. **Mesh** = east-west, internal service-to-service.
- The decision to adopt a mesh is mostly about **service count and team size**, not a fixed rule.
- Most real systems past a certain scale run **both**, each doing the job the other structurally can't.

slides.subTitle: The traffic-direction framing
slides.markdown:
This is the single cleanest way to reason about the decision: a **gateway** handles **north-south** traffic — anything crossing the boundary between your system and the outside world. A **mesh** handles **east-west** traffic — calls between your own services, which never touch the outside world at all.

Most confusion about "do I need a mesh instead of a gateway" resolves once you ask which direction the traffic you're worried about actually flows — they were never solving the same problem.

slides.subTitle: Where a mesh starts paying for itself
slides.markdown:
A gateway is close to always worth it — even one service benefits from centralized auth and rate limiting at the edge. A mesh is different: it adds real operational complexity (another control plane to run, a proxy hop on every call), which only pays off once you have **enough services, in enough languages, owned by enough separate teams** that solving mTLS/retries/observability per-service would be worse.

As a rough signal, teams often start feeling mesh-shaped pain somewhere around **dozens of services** — well before that, a shared library or even hand-rolled retry logic is often simpler and cheaper.

![Gateway at the edge, mesh internally](assets/gateway-and-mesh-together.svg)

A request enters through the gateway once — authenticated, rate-limited — then, once inside, may fan out across many internal service-to-service calls that the mesh secures and observes. The two layers stack cleanly because they own genuinely different traffic.

assets.alt: Gateway at the edge, mesh internally

slides.subTitle: That the other structurally can't
slides.markdown:
| | Gateway | Mesh |
|---|---|---|
| Sees | Only external client requests | Every internal service-to-service call |
| Secures | Client authentication at the edge | mTLS between every internal hop |
| Blind spot | Zero visibility into internal calls | No idea about the original external client |
| Adds per request | One hop, at the edge only | Two hops (caller + callee sidecar), every internal call |

A gateway simply has no visibility past its own boundary; a mesh has no concept of "the original external client" once a request is inside. Neither can substitute for the other's blind spot.

slides.subTitle: A 5-service startup vs a 200-service org
slides.markdown:
| | 5-service startup | 200-service org |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway | Yes — cheap, immediate value | Yes — still needed at the edge |
| Mesh | Usually not — one shared retry/auth library is simpler | Yes — per-service mTLS/observability wouldn't scale across many teams and languages |
| Main risk if wrong | Adopting a mesh too early: unneeded operational overhead | Skipping a mesh too long: inconsistent, duplicated cross-cutting logic across teams |

The same underlying reasoning (gateway almost always yes, mesh scales with service/team count) produces opposite mesh answers depending purely on where the org actually sits on that count.
